questions.question: What is parallel processing?
options: Executing one instruction at a time
questions.explanation: Parallel processing executes multiple instructions or tasks simultaneously using multiple processors or cores.

questions.question: What does a multicore processor have?
options: Multiple independent processing units on one chip
questions.explanation: A multicore processor contains two or more independent processing cores on a single chip, enabling parallel execution.

questions.question: What is SIMD?
questions.explanation: SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data) applies one instruction to multiple data elements simultaneously.

questions.question: What is MIMD?
questions.explanation: MIMD (Multiple Instruction Multiple Data) allows different processors to execute different instructions on different data.

questions.question: What is a thread in computing?
options: A physical wire in the processor
The smallest unit of execution that can be scheduled
questions.explanation: A thread is the smallest sequence of programmed instructions that can be independently scheduled and executed.

questions.question: What is multithreading?
questions.explanation: Multithreading allows a CPU to execute multiple threads concurrently, improving resource utilization.

questions.question: What is speedup in parallel computing?
options: Ratio of serial to parallel execution time
questions.explanation: Speedup measures performance improvement, calculated as sequential time divided by parallel time.

questions.question: What is Amdahl's Law about?
questions.explanation: Amdahl's Law states that speedup is limited by the sequential portion of a program that cannot be parallelized.

questions.question: What is a GPU primarily designed for?
options: Parallel processing of graphics and data
questions.explanation: GPUs are designed for massive parallel processing, particularly for graphics rendering and data-parallel computations.

questions.question: What is task parallelism?
questions.explanation: Task parallelism divides a program into different tasks that can be executed simultaneously on different processors.

questions.question: What does SISD describe in Flynn's taxonomy?
options: Single Instruction Single Data - traditional sequential processing
questions.explanation: SISD is the traditional sequential computer: one instruction stream operating on one data stream.

questions.question: In Flynn's taxonomy, a GPU that applies one instruction to many data elements at once is best classified as what?
questions.explanation: A single instruction operating on many data elements simultaneously is SIMD, the model GPUs follow via SIMT execution.

questions.question: What is MISD in Flynn's taxonomy?
options: Multiple Instruction Single Data - rare, used mainly for fault tolerance
questions.explanation: MISD runs multiple instruction streams on a single data stream; it is uncommon and appears mainly in redundant fault-tolerant systems.

questions.question: What is a computer cluster?
options: A group of connected computers working together as one system
questions.explanation: A cluster links independent computers over a network so they cooperate as a single parallel computing resource.

questions.question: What is a shared-memory multiprocessor?
options: All processors share a common address space
Each processor has completely separate memory
Memory is shared only between two cores
Memory is stored on the network
questions.explanation: In shared-memory systems, all processors access a common address space and communicate through shared variables.

questions.question: How do processors communicate in a distributed-memory system?
options: By passing messages over an interconnect
questions.explanation: Distributed-memory systems give each processor private memory, so they exchange data explicitly via message passing.

questions.question: What is a critical section?
options: The most important part of a program
A code segment that accesses shared resources and must execute atomically
A protected section of the CPU
questions.explanation: A critical section is code touching shared data where only one thread may execute at a time, enforced by locks or other synchronization.

questions.question: What problem does cache coherence address in multiprocessors?
options: Keeping consistent copies of shared data across processor caches
questions.explanation: Cache coherence protocols ensure that when one core updates shared data, other cores' cached copies are updated or invalidated.

questions.question: What is MPI?
options: Message Passing Interface - a standard for distributed parallel programs
questions.explanation: MPI (Message Passing Interface) is the standard library for exchanging data between processes on distributed-memory systems.

questions.question: What is OpenMP used for?
options: Shared-memory parallel programming via compiler directives
questions.explanation: OpenMP uses compiler directives like #pragma omp parallel for to parallelize code on shared-memory systems.

questions.question: What is a vector processor?
options: A processor that handles only vector graphics
A processor performing SIMD operations on entire arrays at once
questions.explanation: Vector processors apply a single instruction to entire vectors (arrays) of data, a classic form of SIMD parallelism used in supercomputers.

questions.question: What does Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT / Hyper-Threading) do?
options: Runs multiple threads on one physical core simultaneously
Splits one thread across multiple cores
Runs exactly one thread per cycle
questions.explanation: SMT lets a single physical core hold multiple thread contexts, filling unused execution slots with work from other threads.

questions.question: What does Gustafson's Law describe?
options: Speedup when problem size is fixed
Scaled speedup when the problem size grows with the number of processors
questions.explanation: Gustafson's Law addresses weak scaling: as processors increase, the problem size grows too, so near-linear speedup becomes achievable.

questions.question: What does GPGPU stand for?
options: General-Purpose computing on Graphics Processing Units
questions.explanation: GPGPU means using graphics processors for general computation (such as CUDA or OpenCL workloads), not just rendering.

questions.question: What does 'embarrassingly parallel' mean?
options: A problem too difficult to parallelize
A problem easily divided into many independent tasks with little communication
A program that embarrasses the programmer
questions.explanation: Embarrassingly parallel problems need little or no inter-task communication, so they scale almost linearly with processors.

questions.question: What does SPMD stand for in parallel programming?
options: Single Program Multiple Data - the same program runs on different data
questions.explanation: SPMD runs copies of one program on many processors, each operating on its own portion of the data.

questions.question: Two threads on different cores repeatedly update different variables that happen to sit in the same cache line, and throughput collapses. What is this called?
questions.explanation: False sharing: the coherence protocol ping-pongs the line between cores even though the variables are logically independent.

questions.question: Which programming model best matches a cluster where every node has private memory and processes exchange explicit messages?
questions.explanation: MPI is designed for distributed memory: no shared address space, all communication via explicit send/receive.

questions.question: According to Amdahl's law, what ultimately limits speedup as processor count grows?
options: The serial fraction of the program
questions.explanation: The non-parallelizable serial fraction bounds speedup at 1/(1-p) no matter how many processors are added.

questions.question: Rendering one million independent pixels, none depending on any other, is best described as what kind of workload?
questions.explanation: Tasks with no inter-task communication or dependencies are embarrassingly parallel and scale nearly linearly.

questions.question: In Flynn's taxonomy, several cores each run different instruction streams on different data (e.g., a multicore server). Which category is this?
questions.explanation: Multiple instruction streams on multiple data streams = MIMD, the class of multicore and multiprocessor systems.
